story.headline: Iran strikes tanker in Strait of Hormuz
story.summary: Iran said its Revolutionary Guard struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker for an 'illegal' Hormuz crossing as shipping fled the strait.
story.display_body: Iran said on Friday 18 September that its Revolutionary Guard had struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker, the _Trend_, for what it called an "illegal attempt" to cross the Strait of Hormuz. State media, cited by the Guard (IRGC — Iran's parallel military and enforcer of the strait blockade), said the vessel caught fire and was detained, and the Guard's navy warned that unauthorised passage would bring the "destruction" of offending ships; The Associated Press said it could not independently confirm the strike. Overnight the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO — a Royal Navy body that tracks Gulf shipping) logged a separate "security incident" 16 nautical miles off Khasab, Oman, with the crew safe and no pollution, and a further report of a tanker hit by an "unknown projectile" that sparked a fire since extinguished — it was not clear whether either matched Iran's claim. Tehran has asserted control over the waterway since the United States and Israel opened their war on Iran on 28 February 2026, and commercial traffic through the strait — which carried close to a fifth of the world's oil before the war — has fallen sharply, pushing Saudi Arabia to route crude through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman instead.
story.why: the Strait of Hormuz is the single most important chokepoint in the global oil trade, and each disputed strike raises both the risk of a wider Gulf confrontation and the price of energy far beyond the region.

story.headline: Russia opens three-day Duma election
story.summary: Russians began a three-day State Duma vote widely described as tightly controlled, as drones were downed over Moscow.
story.display_body: Russians began voting on Friday 18 September in a three-day election for the State Duma, the lower house of the national parliament, with polls due to close on Sunday 20 September. DW and Al Jazeera describe a contest tightly stage-managed by the Kremlin, with the pro-government United Russia party dominant and genuine opposition candidates largely barred or exiled; the "systemic" parties on the ballot broadly back the war in Ukraine. Voting opened as Russian air defences reported downing dozens of Ukrainian drones over the Moscow region overnight.
story.why: the Duma vote is less a real contest than a managed loyalty exercise, but its scale and staging are a read on how the Kremlin wants to project stability at home nineteen months into the war.

story.headline: 37 die in Nigerian mining-arrest custody
story.summary: At least 37 men held for illegal mining died in NSCDC custody in Niger State; officials cite disease, a leaked report cites overcrowding.
story.display_body: At least 37 men arrested for illegal mining died in the custody of Nigeria's Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State, in the country's northeast, and police have opened an investigation, officials said on Thursday 17 September. The men were detained on 15–16 September during an operation against small-scale gold mining in a region known for it; officials attributed the deaths to a disease outbreak, but the AFP news agency cited an intelligence report pointing instead to overcrowding and poor ventilation at the detention facility. The cause remains contested and the bodies have been held pending examination.
story.why: a mass death in state custody, with the official explanation already disputed by leaked findings, points to conditions in Nigeria's detention system that its own security services may be trying to explain away.

story.headline: Gunman kills two at Philippine school
story.summary: A 16-year-old killed two students and wounded eight before shooting himself at a school in South Cotabato, the Philippines' third such attack since June.
story.display_body: A 16-year-old gunman killed at least two students and wounded eight others before shooting himself at a school in Banga, in South Cotabato province in the southern Philippines, on Friday 18 September. Four of the injured were in critical condition and all the victims were aged 14 to 17, provincial and town officials said; the attacker later died. It is the Philippines' third deadly school shooting since June, and officials could not immediately confirm accounts from a teacher of a possible second shooter.

story.headline: Court curbs insurers on hospital planning
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Administrative Court rejected insurers' first challenge to cantonal hospital planning, limiting a new appeal right.
story.display_body: The Federal Administrative Court issued its first-ever ruling on health insurers' new right to challenge cantonal hospital planning on Friday 18 September, rejecting a complaint by the insurers' association Prio.Swiss against the canton of Schwyz. Since 2024 insurer associations have held a Verbandsbeschwerderecht (a collective right of appeal) meant to let them police cantonal hospital lists and curb over-provision and costs; Prio.Swiss used it to argue Schwyz should coordinate its three hospitals' offerings better across cantonal borders. The court declared the appeal inadmissible without ruling on the substance, holding that a whole hospital list cannot be challenged as such — only individual service mandates (the specific treatments a hospital is licensed to provide). As the first judgment on the instrument it sets a precedent (Leiturteil); Prio.Swiss said it may now target individual mandates and questioned whether the appeal right is designed strongly enough to control cantonal planning.
story.why: the ruling narrows a tool insurers had hoped to use to rein in Switzerland's rising health costs, and pushes the fight over hospital over-capacity back toward the cantons and, potentially, parliament.

story.headline: Russia seizes control of Nestlé's units
story.summary: A Putin decree placed Nestlé's Russian operations under state external administration, transferring control to a firm called LEV Management.
story.display_body: A decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on Thursday 17 September placed the Russian operations of Swiss food group Nestlé under temporary "external administration," transferring control of Nestlé Russia and Nestlé Kuban to a Russian firm called LEV Management. The same decree covered the Russian arms of French retailer Auchan and the former Leroy Merlin chain (now Lemana Pro). Nestlé — headquartered in Vevey, canton Vaud — said it had taken note of the decree, was assessing its options and would act to protect its rights and the continuity of a business that employs about 7,000 people across six manufacturing sites and has operated in Russia since 1995; the company remains the legal owner but can no longer make decisions over the units. SRF's Russia correspondent noted that such external administration has in past cases (the Danish brewer Carlsberg, the French dairy group Danone) been a precursor to outright expropriation, with the assets later handed to Kremlin-linked figures.
story.why: it is the latest and one of the largest Western consumer firms to lose operational control of its Russian arm, and a direct hit to a flagship Vaud multinational that had chosen to keep a reduced presence in Russia rather than exit.

story.headline: Study: richest Swiss pay lowest tax rate
story.summary: A St. Gallen/ETH Zurich working paper using distributional national accounts finds Switzerland's top 1% bears the lightest effective tax burden.
story.display_body: A new working paper by economists at the University of St. Gallen and ETH Zurich finds that Switzerland's top 1 percent carry the country's lightest effective tax burden, and that income inequality is larger than tax statistics suggest. "Income, Wealth, and Redistribution in a Tax Haven: Distributional National Accounts for Switzerland," by Enea Baselgia, Remo Gurtner, Julian Koller and Isabel Z. Martínez, builds Distributional National Accounts (DINA — a method pioneered by Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman that starts from the whole economy's income and wealth as measured in the national accounts, rather than from tax returns that miss untaxed corporate profits, pension assets and property value). Covering 2003–2022, it corrects for the profit-shifting that Switzerland's tax-haven status introduces and reweights cantonal tax records to national totals; the effect is to raise the estimated income share of the richest while showing wealth inequality to be somewhat lower than rich-list figures imply.
story.why: the finding cuts against the intuition that a progressive system taxes the wealthiest most, and hands ammunition to a live Swiss debate over whether the very top pays its share.

story.headline: Leysin drops 175-snow-cannon plan
story.summary: A 175-snow-cannon project above Leysin and Les Mosses in Vaud was abandoned after 500-plus objections and protected-marshland law.
story.display_body: The plan to install 175 snow cannons above Leysin and Les Mosses (canton Vaud) has been abandoned, the lift operator Télé Leysin–Les Mosses–La Lécherette confirmed this week. The roughly 20-million-franc scheme drew more than 500 objections in the public inquiry, and part of it sat in the Les Mosses marshland, a wetland of national importance whose federal protection barred the development. The company is refocusing on the Leysin sector alone, where 30 to 40 cannons are now envisaged around the recently rebuilt Aï, Brion, Des Fers and Choulet lifts, with a fresh public inquiry planned before the end of 2026. La Côte, 18 Sep 2026 ; RTS, 2026

story.headline: OpenAI to test ads in ChatGPT
story.summary: OpenAI will test advertising in ChatGPT's free and Go tiers and launch Sponsored Agents.
story.display_body: OpenAI said it will test advertising in ChatGPT's free and lower-cost "Go" tiers in the US, framing ads as a way to subsidize cheaper access worldwide, and separately introduced "Sponsored Agents" plus advertiser tooling and integrations with HubSpot and Shopify. The company says it will protect privacy and keep ads from degrading answer quality.
story.why: the largest consumer AI product tilting toward an ad-funded model is a structural shift with the same tensions that shaped search and social — the incentive to optimize a supposedly neutral assistant's answers for advertisers now sits directly against the product's usefulness. How OpenAI walls off ranking from answers, and whether it discloses paid placement clearly, is the thing to watch as the test rolls out.

story.headline: What actually makes a coding agent work
story.summary: A component-level study isolates planning, action space and context management in coding-agent harnesses on SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench.
story.display_body: A coding harness is the scaffolding around a model that turns it into an autonomous software engineer — the loop that plans, runs commands, reads files, and decides when the task is done. Most work treats the harness as one indivisible black box; this paper instead freezes the execution loop and varies three components in isolation — planning, action space, and context management — across four models on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (standard suites of real GitHub-issue and terminal tasks), over 176 matched settings.
story.why: the findings are directly actionable for anyone building agents. Context management earns its keep mainly by preventing context-overflow crashes, and cheap rule-based trimming before an LLM-written summary beats fancier schemes; planning is an accuracy crutch for weaker models but a pure cost-saver for stronger ones; and bash-capable models run just as well — and far cheaper — with a plain shell instead of a bespoke toolset. It is a modular framework for evaluating harness pieces rather than guessing.

story.headline: DeepSeek details its 552B V4.1-Flash
story.summary: DeepSeek's architecture paper explains how V4.1-Flash cuts its KV cache to 890 bytes per token for million-token contexts.
story.display_body: The open weights landed earlier this month (covered in the 12 September Weekend brief); this is the technical paper that explains how. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is a 552B-parameter multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model (MoE — only a small subset of "expert" sub-networks fire per token) supporting one-million-token contexts. Its Causal Encoder-Decoder design activates 16B parameters per token when generating but only 8B when ingesting the prompt, and it stacks cross-layer KV-cache reuse with FP4 (4-bit) caching to cut the always-in-memory KV footprint to 890 bytes per token — roughly a quarter of its predecessor's — while a deployment trick called SWA Bounded Replay cuts the on-disk footprint to about an eighth.
story.why: input-heavy agent workloads, not chat, now dominate serving cost, and the KV cache is the wall they hit. An open-weight reference design that quarters that footprint without losing quality sets a concrete efficiency bar competitors and self-hosters will measure against.

story.headline: Models learn when to read their history
story.summary: On-Demand Attention trains a recall head so a model invokes costly global attention only when it helps.
story.display_body: Standard decoding re-reads the entire growing history at every generated token, whether or not that global read changes the next word. On-Demand Attention (ODA) trains a small "recall head" that predicts, from the model's own decoding state, whether a global read will help right now — and otherwise falls back to cheap local attention. Only the recall head is trained; the pretrained weights and the full KV cache stay intact, so nothing is lost, just deferred. The authors add GPU-side conditional execution in vLLM (a widely used inference server) so the saved reads become real speedups at long context.
story.why: it recovers most of the accuracy that naive local-attention shortcuts throw away while cutting the expensive global reads — a rare efficiency lever that needs no retraining of the base model and ships as a practical kernel, not just a plot.

story.headline: Reasoning models learn when to think
story.summary: When2Think post-trains reasoning models to spend compute by problem difficulty, cutting tokens while raising accuracy.
story.display_body: Large reasoning models systematically overthink easy questions and underthink hard ones, burning tokens on the former and accuracy on the latter. When2Think is a post-training recipe whose core mechanism, Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control, shapes the reward using pre-computed reference statistics (how accurate and how long typical answers are) so the model learns to answer directly on easy items and reason at length on hard ones — a learned System 1 / System 2 switch.
story.why: on the AIME24 math competition benchmark it lifts Pass@3 (fraction solved within three tries) by 10.0% while using 27.9% fewer tokens than the base model — a real both-directions win rather than the usual accuracy-for-speed trade, and it needs no separate learned reward model.

story.headline: Entropy coding shrinks the KV cache
story.summary: D-Quant applies entropy coding to KV-cache quantization and repacks it into GPU-friendly fixed-size blocks.
story.display_body: Most KV-cache compression uses fixed-width quantization: every value gets the same b bits, capping it at 2^b levels, and quality collapses as b shrinks. The authors note that after rotation and normalization the cached values are roughly bell-curved — most near the centre, few in the tails — so fixed-width coding wastes bits on rare values. D-Quant instead applies entropy coding (short codes for common values, long codes for rare ones), then adds a "drift" mechanism that repacks the variable-length output into fixed-size blocks so GPU attention kernels can still do the regular, parallel memory access they need.
story.why: it squeezes the same information into fewer average bits and keeps the layout GPUs can actually run fast on — the practical catch that has sunk earlier entropy-coding attempts.

story.headline: Diffusion LMs from hybrid backbones
story.summary: dQwen3.5 adapts hybrid attention-RNN Qwen models into diffusion language models at half the training tokens.
story.display_body: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising many positions in parallel rather than strictly left-to-right, and the cheap way to build one is to adapt an existing autoregressive model. Almost all such adaptations start from a pure-attention Transformer; modern models increasingly interleave attention with RNN layers, which are structurally one-directional and awkward to convert. This paper shows it works anyway, adapting Qwen3.5 at 0.8B–9B scales into the dQwen3.5 family.
story.why: the hybrid backbone reaches a given training loss in roughly half the tokens of a full-attention control, so the architecture the field is already moving toward turns out to be a cheaper, not harder, starting point for parallel-decoding models.

story.headline: LLMs may hold alien concepts
story.summary: A position paper argues LLMs encode 'xeno-representations' — distinctions no human concept captures — with safety implications.
story.display_body: Interpretability usually hunts for human ideas inside a model — truthfulness, deception, refusal. This position paper argues the model's internal space of distinctions is far larger than the finite set humans can describe, and names the leftover region "xeno-representations": structures you can reproducibly locate, geometrically characterize, causally poke, and tie to behaviour, even when you cannot say in words what they mean.
story.why: if models act on distinctions with no human-readable label — and those distinctions can spread and stabilize across cooperating agents — then interpretability aimed only at human concepts has a permanent blind spot, which is a real (if still speculative) safety concern for multi-agent systems.

story.headline: LLM groups manufacture false consensus
story.summary: Matched LLM agent groups reach full consensus far more than humans on the same reasoning task — often on wrong answers.
story.display_body: Simulated "agent societies" are increasingly used to stand in for human groups, so it matters how faithfully they reproduce human disagreement. The author replayed 100 held-out human groups solving the Wason task (a classic logical-reasoning puzzle), seeding a matched LLM agent for each participant's starting belief and scoring both with the same code. Agent groups reached full consensus 34–44 percentage points more often than the humans, and under a reasoning mode they agreed almost unanimously — mostly on wrong answers.
story.why: consensus among LLM agents did not track whether they were correct, so treating multi-agent agreement as a signal of collective intelligence — or as a stand-in for human deliberation — is unfounded in this setting.

story.headline: OpenAI publishes misalignment reports
story.summary: OpenAI released a framework for disclosing model misalignment plus six reports of concerning behaviour.
story.display_body: OpenAI released a framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing model misalignment — cases where a model pursues something other than what its developers or users intend — alongside six concrete reports of unexpected or concerning behaviour it has observed. It is paired with a companion post on monitoring OpenAI's own internal coding agents via chain-of-thought inspection (reading the model's step-by-step reasoning trace for warning signs).
story.why: it is a rare instance of a frontier lab standardizing how it reports its own models misbehaving rather than only publishing capability wins. The disclosures are self-selected and unaudited — take them as a governance gesture, not independent verification — but a shared reporting template is a precondition for outside scrutiny later.

story.headline: Iran strikes tanker in Strait of Hormuz
story.summary: Iran said its Revolutionary Guard struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker for an 'illegal' Hormuz crossing as shipping fled the strait.
story.display_body: Iran said on Friday 18 September that its Revolutionary Guard had struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker, the _Trend_, for what it called an "illegal attempt" to cross the Strait of Hormuz. State media, cited by the Guard (IRGC — Iran's parallel military and enforcer of the strait blockade), said the vessel caught fire and was detained, and the Guard's navy warned that unauthorised passage would bring the "destruction" of offending ships; The Associated Press said it could not independently confirm the strike. Overnight the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO — a Royal Navy body that tracks Gulf shipping) logged a separate "security incident" 16 nautical miles off Khasab, Oman, with the crew safe and no pollution, and a further report of a tanker hit by an "unknown projectile" that sparked a fire since extinguished — it was not clear whether either matched Iran's claim. Tehran has asserted control over the waterway since the United States and Israel opened their war on Iran on 28 February 2026, and commercial traffic through the strait — which carried close to a fifth of the world's oil before the war — has fallen sharply, pushing Saudi Arabia to route crude through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman instead.
story.why: the Strait of Hormuz is the single most important chokepoint in the global oil trade, and each disputed strike raises both the risk of a wider Gulf confrontation and the price of energy far beyond the region.

story.headline: Russia opens three-day Duma election
story.summary: Russians began a three-day State Duma vote widely described as tightly controlled, as drones were downed over Moscow.
story.display_body: Russians began voting on Friday 18 September in a three-day election for the State Duma, the lower house of the national parliament, with polls due to close on Sunday 20 September. DW and Al Jazeera describe a contest tightly stage-managed by the Kremlin, with the pro-government United Russia party dominant and genuine opposition candidates largely barred or exiled; the "systemic" parties on the ballot broadly back the war in Ukraine. Voting opened as Russian air defences reported downing dozens of Ukrainian drones over the Moscow region overnight.
story.why: the Duma vote is less a real contest than a managed loyalty exercise, but its scale and staging are a read on how the Kremlin wants to project stability at home nineteen months into the war.

story.headline: 37 die in Nigerian mining-arrest custody
story.summary: At least 37 men held for illegal mining died in NSCDC custody in Niger State; officials cite disease, a leaked report cites overcrowding.
story.display_body: At least 37 men arrested for illegal mining died in the custody of Nigeria's Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State, in the country's northeast, and police have opened an investigation, officials said on Thursday 17 September. The men were detained on 15–16 September during an operation against small-scale gold mining in a region known for it; officials attributed the deaths to a disease outbreak, but the AFP news agency cited an intelligence report pointing instead to overcrowding and poor ventilation at the detention facility. The cause remains contested and the bodies have been held pending examination.
story.why: a mass death in state custody, with the official explanation already disputed by leaked findings, points to conditions in Nigeria's detention system that its own security services may be trying to explain away.

story.headline: Gunman kills two at Philippine school
story.summary: A 16-year-old killed two students and wounded eight before shooting himself at a school in South Cotabato, the Philippines' third such attack since June.
story.display_body: A 16-year-old gunman killed at least two students and wounded eight others before shooting himself at a school in Banga, in South Cotabato province in the southern Philippines, on Friday 18 September. Four of the injured were in critical condition and all the victims were aged 14 to 17, provincial and town officials said; the attacker later died. It is the Philippines' third deadly school shooting since June, and officials could not immediately confirm accounts from a teacher of a possible second shooter.

story.headline: Court curbs insurers on hospital planning
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Administrative Court rejected insurers' first challenge to cantonal hospital planning, limiting a new appeal right.
story.display_body: The Federal Administrative Court issued its first-ever ruling on health insurers' new right to challenge cantonal hospital planning on Friday 18 September, rejecting a complaint by the insurers' association Prio.Swiss against the canton of Schwyz. Since 2024 insurer associations have held a Verbandsbeschwerderecht (a collective right of appeal) meant to let them police cantonal hospital lists and curb over-provision and costs; Prio.Swiss used it to argue Schwyz should coordinate its three hospitals' offerings better across cantonal borders. The court declared the appeal inadmissible without ruling on the substance, holding that a whole hospital list cannot be challenged as such — only individual service mandates (the specific treatments a hospital is licensed to provide). As the first judgment on the instrument it sets a precedent (Leiturteil); Prio.Swiss said it may now target individual mandates and questioned whether the appeal right is designed strongly enough to control cantonal planning.
story.why: the ruling narrows a tool insurers had hoped to use to rein in Switzerland's rising health costs, and pushes the fight over hospital over-capacity back toward the cantons and, potentially, parliament.

story.headline: Russia seizes control of Nestlé's units
story.summary: A Putin decree placed Nestlé's Russian operations under state external administration, transferring control to a firm called LEV Management.
story.display_body: A decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on Thursday 17 September placed the Russian operations of Swiss food group Nestlé under temporary "external administration," transferring control of Nestlé Russia and Nestlé Kuban to a Russian firm called LEV Management. The same decree covered the Russian arms of French retailer Auchan and the former Leroy Merlin chain (now Lemana Pro). Nestlé — headquartered in Vevey, canton Vaud — said it had taken note of the decree, was assessing its options and would act to protect its rights and the continuity of a business that employs about 7,000 people across six manufacturing sites and has operated in Russia since 1995; the company remains the legal owner but can no longer make decisions over the units. SRF's Russia correspondent noted that such external administration has in past cases (the Danish brewer Carlsberg, the French dairy group Danone) been a precursor to outright expropriation, with the assets later handed to Kremlin-linked figures.
story.why: it is the latest and one of the largest Western consumer firms to lose operational control of its Russian arm, and a direct hit to a flagship Vaud multinational that had chosen to keep a reduced presence in Russia rather than exit.

story.headline: Study: richest Swiss pay lowest tax rate
story.summary: A St. Gallen/ETH Zurich working paper using distributional national accounts finds Switzerland's top 1% bears the lightest effective tax burden.
story.display_body: A new working paper by economists at the University of St. Gallen and ETH Zurich finds that Switzerland's top 1 percent carry the country's lightest effective tax burden, and that income inequality is larger than tax statistics suggest. "Income, Wealth, and Redistribution in a Tax Haven: Distributional National Accounts for Switzerland," by Enea Baselgia, Remo Gurtner, Julian Koller and Isabel Z. Martínez, builds Distributional National Accounts (DINA — a method pioneered by Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman that starts from the whole economy's income and wealth as measured in the national accounts, rather than from tax returns that miss untaxed corporate profits, pension assets and property value). Covering 2003–2022, it corrects for the profit-shifting that Switzerland's tax-haven status introduces and reweights cantonal tax records to national totals; the effect is to raise the estimated income share of the richest while showing wealth inequality to be somewhat lower than rich-list figures imply.
story.why: the finding cuts against the intuition that a progressive system taxes the wealthiest most, and hands ammunition to a live Swiss debate over whether the very top pays its share. Working paper — Baselgia, Gurtner, Koller & Martínez, 2026

story.headline: Leysin drops 175-snow-cannon plan
story.summary: A 175-snow-cannon project above Leysin and Les Mosses in Vaud was abandoned after 500-plus objections and protected-marshland law.
story.display_body: The plan to install 175 snow cannons above Leysin and Les Mosses (canton Vaud) has been abandoned, the lift operator Télé Leysin–Les Mosses–La Lécherette confirmed this week. The roughly 20-million-franc scheme drew more than 500 objections in the public inquiry, and part of it sat in the Les Mosses marshland, a wetland of national importance whose federal protection barred the development. The company is refocusing on the Leysin sector alone, where 30 to 40 cannons are now envisaged around the recently rebuilt Aï, Brion, Des Fers and Choulet lifts, with a fresh public inquiry planned before the end of 2026. La Côte, 18 Sep 2026 ; RTS, 2026
